newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 hits record on Wall St surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK's FTSE 100 hits record on Wall St surge.

text.p: An overnight surge on Wall Street propelled British shares to a record high at the start of trading on Friday, with the blue-chip FTSE 100 index hitting a peak 11 percent above its level at the end of 1995.
After rising as high as 4,097.1 at the start of trading, thrusting past its previous peak of 4,094.4 set on November 26, the index was up 25.1 points at 4,076.4 by 1145 GMT.
It was the latest surge on Wall Street, where the Dow recorded its second-biggest one-day gain ever with a rise of 126.87 points, that gave the London market a boost.
"The Dow's jump overnight was unbelievable," said one senior dealer in London. "It certainly has given the market a boost of confidence."
Other European markets also rose sharply, with Germany's Dax for instance rising 41.13 points or 1.5 percent to 2,848.85 by 1131 GMT.
Friday's surge added another leg to the UK market's long-awaited year-end rally, usually attributed to seasonal inflows of cash into investment fund coffers.

And with a recent spate of takeover bids promising to inject further cash into the market, as well as prompting further gains in other possible bid targets, traders and analysts said the FTSE could push towards 4,200 before the year is out.
Yet they said major uncertainties remained over the outlook for 1997 -- and that the higher the index goes before year end, the more likely a consolidation becomes in the first part of the new year.
Recent proliferating signs that UK economic growth is gaining pace are expected to force Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates in the first quarter of the new year.

And with Prime Minister John Major's parliamentary majority already wiped out, concern is likely to grow over the timing of the general election which must be held by the end of May -- and which the opposition Labour Party is well placed to win.
"All those uncertainties may well create a period of consolidation at the start of 1997," said the head of equity trading at one brokerage.
Recent weeks have seen a volatile performance in world markets as investors weigh up prospects for 1997.

Just two weeks ago shares and bonds around the world were spooked by comments from Alan Greenspan, head of the U.S. central bank, warning against the "irrational exhuberance" that he saw gripping markets.

The implicit threat was that Greenspan would raise interest rates if he thought there was a real risk of rampant markets pushing up inflation, and the FTSE plummeted to its lowest level in three months the day after his comments.
Yet markets have rallied back in recent sessions as Wall Street recovered from its bout of jitters to push back to near record levels in recent sessions.

Today's opening surge was exaggerated as dealers at leading brokerages, left short of stock after recent unexpected demand, quoted prices sharply higher in a manoeuvre designed partly to deter buyers and shake out some sellers of stock.
Many investors remain cautious over the outlook for 1997, yet once the UK election is out of the way, some believe London might actually outperform other European markets through the year as a whole.
"There probably is value to be revealed in the UK market," said Steve Wright, investment strategist at brokerage BZW, "but that will probably not appear until after the election."
